lessons.title: Introduction and Why It Matters
lessons.body: TIG welding, or Tungsten Inert Gas welding, is a precise method that uses a non-consumable tungsten electrode to create an arc that melts the base metal. A separate filler rod is added by hand. This gives you control that stick or MIG welding can't match. In Africa, TIG is in high demand for food-grade stainless steel in dairy and brewery plants, aluminium in auto repair and window fabrication, and thin sheet metal in artisan workshops. For example, in Kenya's growing solar panel industry, TIG is used to weld aluminium frames that must be watertight and corrosion-resistant. Learning TIG opens doors to higher-paying jobs because it requires skill and patience. Unlike stick welding, TIG produces clean, spatter-free welds that often need no grinding. That saves time and money. But it's slower and demands good hand-eye coordination. You'll need a TIG machine with high-frequency start, a gas cylinder of 100% argon, and a regulator. In many African cities, you can find used TIG machines for around $300-$600. The gas costs about $50-$80 per refill, but a cylinder lasts many hours. TIG is also versatile: you can weld steel, stainless steel, aluminium, copper, and even titanium. For a self-employed welder, TIG means you can take on repair jobs for restaurants, dairies, and factories that need sanitary welds. This module will teach you from the ground up: tools, technique, fixing mistakes, safety, and a practical exercise. By the end, you'll be able to lay a clean bead on mild steel and stainless steel, and you'll know how to troubleshoot common problems. TIG is a skill that pays for itself quickly if you practice. Let's get started.

lessons.title: Tools and Materials
lessons.body: To TIG weld, you need the right equipment. First, a TIG welder. Look for one with adjustable amperage (at least 200A for aluminium) and high-frequency start. Inverters are lighter and more energy-efficient. Brands like Miller, Lincoln, or cheaper Chinese units like Everlast are common in Africa. Next, a tungsten electrode. For steel and stainless, use 2% thoriated (red) or ceriated (grey) tungsten. For aluminium, pure tungsten (green) works but lanthanated (gold) is better. You'll need a tungsten grinder or a dedicated grinding wheel to sharpen the tip. Never use the same wheel for steel. Shielding gas: 100% argon for most metals. For thicker aluminium, you can use a helium-argon mix, but argon is fine up to 6mm. Gas flow rate: 10-15 cubic feet per hour (CFH) for most jobs. A flowmeter is essential. Filler rods: for mild steel, use ER70S-6; for stainless, ER308L; for aluminium, ER4043 or ER5356. Sizes: 1.6mm, 2.4mm, and 3.2mm. You'll also need a welding helmet with a shade 9-13 lens, TIG gloves (thin and flexible), and a torch with a collet body, collet, and ceramic cup. Cups come in sizes #4 to #8; #6 is a good all-rounder. A foot pedal is highly recommended for amperage control. For cleaning, have a stainless steel wire brush (dedicated to aluminium only) and acetone or alcohol for wiping oil. In Africa, you can source these from welding supply shops in major cities or online. A basic TIG setup costs around $500-$1000. Don't skimp on gas quality; moisture in gas causes porosity. Keep your tungsten sharp and your metal clean. That's half the battle.

lessons.title: Step by Step Method
lessons.body: Start by cleaning your metal. Remove all oil, paint, and rust with acetone and a stainless brush. For aluminium, brush with a dedicated stainless brush until shiny. Set up your machine: for 3mm mild steel, set amperage to 80-100A; for 3mm stainless, 60-80A; for 3mm aluminium, 120-150A. Set gas flow to 12 CFH. Sharpen your tungsten to a point (for steel) or a balled tip (for aluminium). Clamp your work lead to the table or workpiece. Put on your helmet and gloves. Hold the torch like a pencil, with the cup resting on the metal if possible. Press the foot pedal to start the arc. Keep a short arc length (1-2mm). For steel, make a small puddle, then dip the filler rod into the leading edge of the puddle. Move forward steadily, dipping and moving. For a bead on plate, travel speed should be about 2-3mm per second. For a butt joint, tack the ends first, then weld from one end to the other. Use a slight forward push angle (10-15 degrees). For aluminium, you need to move faster and use more heat. The puddle should be shiny and fluid. Dip the filler as soon as the puddle forms. If you see black soot, you're too hot or moving too slow. For stainless, keep the heat low and move quickly to avoid warping. After welding, let the post-flow gas run for a few seconds to cool the tungsten. Practice on scrap metal first. Make 10 beads on a flat plate before trying joints. Remember: TIG is about consistency. Keep your arc length constant and your dip rhythm steady. A good exercise is to weld a series of overlapping beads, then cut and etch to see penetration. In Africa, many welders learn by doing repairs on pots, pans, and gates. Start with thin material and work up.

lessons.title: Common Mistakes and Fixes
lessons.body: Mistake 1: Tungsten touching the puddle. This contaminates the tungsten and causes a sputtery arc. Fix: Sharpen the tungsten again and restart. Keep a short arc but don't dip the tungsten. Mistake 2: Porosity (holes in the weld). Causes: dirty metal, low gas flow, or too much arc length. Fix: Clean with acetone, increase gas to 15 CFH, and shorten arc. Mistake 3: Lack of penetration. You're moving too fast or amps too low. Fix: Increase amps by 10-20A and slow down. For 3mm steel, you need at least 80A. Mistake 4: Burn-through on thin metal. Too many amps or too slow. Fix: Reduce amps, use a faster travel speed, or use a heat sink (copper backing). Mistake 5: Tungsten balling up on steel. This happens if you use pure tungsten on steel. Fix: Use 2% thoriated or ceriated tungsten. Mistake 6: Arc wandering. This is often due to a bent tungsten or wrong grind angle. Fix: Grind tungsten longitudinally, not radially, and keep it straight. Mistake 7: Black soot on aluminium. This is from too much heat or not enough cleaning. Fix: Reduce amps, increase travel speed, and brush the aluminium right before welding. Mistake 8: Cracking in stainless. This can happen from too much heat or fast cooling. Fix: Use less amps, backstep weld, or use a chill block. Mistake 9: Gas leaks. Check hose connections with soapy water. Replace cracked hoses. Mistake 10: Inconsistent bead. This is from poor hand position. Fix: Rest your hand on a block or use a torch guide. Practice makes perfect. In Africa, where materials can be expensive, always test on scrap first. Learn to read the puddle: it should be a calm, shiny pool. If it's turbulent, something is wrong. Keep a notebook of settings that work for different thicknesses. That's how you become a pro.

lessons.title: Safety and Best Practice
lessons.body: TIG welding is safer than stick welding because there's no slag and less spatter, but hazards still exist. The arc emits intense ultraviolet (UV) and infrared light. Always wear a welding helmet with a proper shade. For TIG at 100A, use shade 10; for 200A, shade 12. Never look at the arc with naked eyes. Wear flame-resistant clothing, leather gloves, and a leather apron. TIG gloves are thin for dexterity, but they still protect from heat and UV. Ensure good ventilation. TIG welding produces ozone and nitrogen oxides, especially on aluminium. In a small workshop, use a fume extractor or open windows and doors. Never weld in a closed room. Argon gas is heavier than air and can displace oxygen. If you're welding in a pit or confined space, use a respirator and have someone watch you. Keep a fire extinguisher nearby. The arc can ignite flammable materials. Clear the area of paper, cloth, and solvents. Electrical safety: check your cables for damage. Don't weld in wet conditions. Use a GFCI if possible. Ground the workpiece properly. When not welding, turn off the machine and close the gas valve. Store gas cylinders upright and secure them with a chain. Never roll a cylinder on its side. In Africa, power fluctuations can damage inverters. Use a surge protector or voltage stabilizer. Best practices: Keep your tungsten sharp and clean. Use the right gas flow. Don't overheat the metal; it can warp or crack. Let the weld cool before handling. Clean your work area daily. Wear safety glasses when grinding tungsten. And always practice good posture to avoid back strain. TIG welding can be done for hours, so take breaks. Drink water. Remember, safety is not just for you; it's for everyone in the shop. A safe welder is a productive welder.

lessons.title: Practical Exercise
lessons.body: For this exercise, you'll need: a TIG welder, 3mm mild steel plate (100mm x 100mm), ER70S-6 filler rod (2.4mm), argon gas, a #6 cup, 2% thoriated tungsten (2.4mm), a stainless brush, acetone, and a grinder. First, clean the steel with acetone and brush off any rust. Set your machine to DCEN (direct current electrode negative) for steel. Set amperage to 90A. Set gas flow to 12 CFH. Sharpen your tungsten to a sharp point. Clamp the plate to your table. Put on your helmet and gloves. Step 1: Make a bead on plate without filler. Practice moving the torch in a straight line, creating a puddle. Keep arc length 2mm. Do this for 5 passes. Step 2: Add filler. Hold the filler rod at a 15-degree angle. Dip the rod into the leading edge of the puddle, then move forward. Dip every 2-3mm. Aim for a consistent bead width of 4-5mm. Do 10 beads. Step 3: Butt joint. Cut two plates, place them with a 1mm gap, tack both ends. Weld from one end to the other. Use the same dip technique. Check penetration by cutting the weld crosswise and polishing with a grinder. You want full penetration without burn-through. Step 4: T-joint. Stand one plate on another and weld the corner. This is harder; use 80A and move faster. Step 5: Aluminium practice (optional). If you have aluminium, set to AC, use pure tungsten, and 120A. Clean with a stainless brush, weld a bead. After each step, inspect your weld. Look for undercut, porosity, and consistency. Write down the settings that worked. Repeat until you can make a clean bead without stopping. In Africa, you can use scrap metal from car panels or roofing sheets. Practice for at least 2 hours. This exercise builds muscle memory. When you can weld a butt joint on 3mm steel that passes a bend test, you're ready for real jobs.

lessons.title: Practical Reference
lessons.body:
Practical Reference: TIG Welding in an African Agribusiness Context

TIG (Tungsten Inert Gas) welding â also called GTAW (Gas Tungsten Arc Welding) â is the precision instrument of metal joining. For African agribusinesses, it is the technique that turns a workshop into a revenue centre: repairing stainless steel milk lines in Kenya, fabricating aluminium irrigation manifolds in Zambia, building food-grade processing tanks in Nigeria, or restoring tractor hydraulic fittings in Tanzania. This Practical Reference consolidates the tools, parameters, defect remedies and safety controls you need to quote, weld and deliver TIG work profitably. Treat it as your bench-side companion during the Practical Exercise and beyond.

Core Process Parameters

Parameter selection separates a profitable TIG shop from a frustrated one. The table below gives starting points for the materials most common in African agribusiness fabrication â mild steel frames, stainless dairy and food equipment, and aluminium irrigation components. Always verify against the filler manufacturer's data sheet and do a test coupon before committing to a customer's part.

Table 1: Typical DCEN TIG parameters for common agribusiness materials (1.6 mm tungsten, argon shielding)
Material Thickness Current (A) Filler rod Argon flow (L/min)
Mild steel1.5 mm60â80ER70S-2 (1.6 mm)8â10
Mild steel3.0 mm90â120ER70S-2 (2.4 mm)10â12
Stainless 3041.5 mm55â75ER308L (1.6 mm)8â10
Stainless 3043.0 mm85â110ER308L (2.4 mm)10â12
Aluminium 6061 (AC)3.0 mm120â150ER4043 (2.4 mm)12â15

Source: adapted from Lincoln Electric, GTAW Welding Guide (Cleveland, OH), and Miller Electric, TIG Welding Handbook. Values are starting points; joint design, position and travel speed will shift them.

Common Defects, Causes and Business Consequences

Every defect is a cost: rework hours, wasted gas, lost customer trust. The table below links the defect to its root cause and the shop-floor correction â so a supervisor can diagnose from the bench, not from a textbook.

Table 2: TIG defect diagnosis and corrective action
Defect Likely cause Corrective action Cost impact if ignored
Porosity Damp filler, dirty base metal, low gas flow or draughts Clean with acetone, dry filler, raise flow to 10â12 L/min, shield from wind Leaks in milk or water lines; rework and warranty claims
Oxidised / black weld Insufficient shielding, wrong polarity, excessive heat Check gas cup size, use DCEN on steel, reduce amperage, add trailing shield Rejection on food-grade stainless; corrosion risk
Tungsten contamination Electrode touched pool or filler; wrong tungsten type Re-grind tungsten longitudinally, use 2% lanthanated on AC, keep 2â3 mm arc gap Weld restarts, arc wander, lost time per joint
Incomplete fusion Low current, fast travel, poor joint prep Increase amperage 10â15%, slow travel, bevel and clean edges Structural failure in tractor or trailer repairs â liability
Burn-through Excess current, slow travel, thin material Reduce amperage, increase travel speed, use heat sink or backing Scrapped sheet metal; wasted stainless stock

Source: compiled from AWS Welding Handbook Vol. 2 and Lincoln Electric GTAW troubleshooting guidance.

â  SAFETY WARNING â TIG welding hazards
  • Electric shock: TIG uses high-frequency (HF) starting. Never weld in wet boots or on damp ground â common during rainy seasons. Use a dry insulating mat and check the earth clamp.
  • UV radiation: The TIG arc emits intense UV. Always use a shade 10â13 helmet with correct filter. Bare skin will burn within minutes.
  • Argon asphyxiation: Argon is heavier than air and displaces oxygen in confined workshops, pits or tanks. Ventilate enclosed spaces and never weld inside a sealed vessel without forced extraction.
  • Fumes: Stainless welding releases hexavalent chromium and nickel. Use local exhaust ventilation or a powered air-purifying respirator (PAPR).
  • Fire: Sparks can ignite dry grass, maize husks or diesel spills common in agri workshops. Keep a dry-powder extinguisher within 3 metres and clear combustibles from the bench.

Quick Reference Checklist

  • Prepare the metal: Degrease with acetone, grind to bright metal, bevel joints >3 mm.
  • Select tungsten: 2% lanthanated for AC/DC general work; grind longitudinally to a sharp point.
  • Set gas flow: 8â12 L/min argon; increase to 14 L/min for aluminium or outdoor draughts.
  • Check polarity: DCEN for steel and stainless; AC for aluminium.
  • Maintain arc length: 2â3 mm, short enough to hear a steady hiss, not a crackle.
  • Feed filler consistently: dip at the leading edge of the pool, withdraw before moving.
  • Control heat input: use foot pedal or amperage control to taper off and avoid crater cracks.
  • Post-weld: brush stainless with a dedicated stainless brush; inspect for porosity before signing off.

Further Reading

  • American Welding Society (AWS) â free technical resources, safety fact sheets and the Welding Handbook reference material.
  • Lincoln Electric â Education & Welding Guides â free downloadable GTAW guides and parameter charts.
  • Miller Electric â Resource Library â TIG welding handbooks, defect troubleshooting and videos.
  • OSHA â Welding, Cutting and Brazing Safety â free e-tools and hazard guidance applicable to African workshop HSE plans.
  • International Labour Organization (ILO) â occupational safety and health resources for informal and small-scale metalwork enterprises.

Business note: In markets such as Kenya, Nigeria, Ghana and South Africa, TIG capability opens doors to higher-value work â food-grade stainless fabrication, dairy and beverage plant maintenance, aluminium irrigation and solar mounting structures. Price TIG by the joint complexity, not just by the hour: a clean, defect-free weld on a milk line is worth more than three rushed ones. Train your team on this reference, log every defect, and use the checklist as a pre-quote quality gate.

quiz.q: What does TIG stand for?
quiz.explanation: TIG stands for Tungsten Inert Gas, referring to the non-consumable tungsten electrode and inert shielding gas.

quiz.q: Which gas is most commonly used for TIG welding?
quiz.explanation: Argon is an inert gas that shields the weld from contamination and is suitable for most TIG applications.

quiz.q: What is the purpose of a foot pedal in TIG welding?
quiz.explanation: A foot pedal allows the welder to adjust amperage while welding, providing better heat control.

quiz.q: Which tungsten electrode is best for welding steel?
quiz.explanation: 2% thoriated tungsten maintains a sharp tip and handles high amperage well, making it ideal for steel.

quiz.q: What is the recommended gas flow rate for most TIG welding?
quiz.explanation: 10-15 cubic feet per hour provides adequate shielding without wasting gas or causing turbulence.

quiz.q: What type of current is used for TIG welding aluminium?
quiz.explanation: Alternating current (AC) helps break up the oxide layer on aluminium and provides cleaning action.

quiz.q: What is the correct filler rod for mild steel TIG welding?
quiz.explanation: ER70S-6 is a common mild steel filler rod that provides good strength and ductility.

quiz.q: What should you do if your tungsten touches the weld puddle?
options: C) Stop, regrind tungsten, and restart
quiz.explanation: Touching the puddle contaminates the tungsten, causing an unstable arc, so it must be reground.

quiz.q: What causes porosity in a TIG weld?
options: B) Dirty metal or low gas flow
quiz.explanation: Porosity is often caused by contamination from dirt, oil, or inadequate shielding gas coverage.

quiz.q: What is the recommended arc length for TIG welding?
quiz.explanation: A short arc length of 1-2mm maintains a focused arc and good shielding.

quiz.q: Why should you use a stainless steel brush on aluminium before welding?
quiz.explanation: Aluminium forms a tough oxide layer that must be removed to prevent porosity and ensure good fusion.

quiz.q: What is the correct shade lens for TIG welding at 100A?
quiz.explanation: Shade 10 is recommended for TIG welding at 100A to protect eyes from UV and infrared radiation.

quiz.q: What is a common cause of burn-through on thin metal?
quiz.explanation: Excessive amperage overheats the metal, causing it to melt through; reduce amps or increase travel speed.

quiz.q: What is the purpose of post-flow gas in TIG welding?
options: A) To cool the tungsten and shield the weld
quiz.explanation: Post-flow continues gas flow after the arc stops to protect the hot tungsten and weld from oxidation.

quiz.q: Which type of tungsten is best for aluminium?
quiz.explanation: Pure tungsten balls up nicely on AC and provides a stable arc for aluminium welding.

quiz.q: What is the recommended amperage for 3mm mild steel TIG welding?
quiz.explanation: 80-100A provides sufficient heat to fuse 3mm steel without burn-through.

quiz.q: What is a common mistake when welding stainless steel?
quiz.explanation: Stainless steel is prone to warping and cracking if overheated, so use lower amperage and faster travel.

quiz.q: Why is it important to grind tungsten longitudinally?
quiz.explanation: Longitudinal grinding creates a stable arc that stays focused on the weld joint.

quiz.q: What should you do if you see black soot on an aluminium weld?
options: B) Reduce heat and clean metal
quiz.explanation: Black soot indicates excessive heat or inadequate cleaning; reduce amps and brush the metal.

quiz.q: What is the correct way to store gas cylinders?
quiz.explanation: Cylinders should be stored upright and chained to prevent falling and damaging the valve.

quiz.q: What is a good practice before TIG welding?
options: A) Clean the metal with acetone
C) Weld in a closed room
quiz.explanation: Cleaning with acetone removes oils and contaminants that cause porosity.

quiz.q: What is the purpose of a collet in a TIG torch?
quiz.explanation: The collet grips the tungsten electrode and ensures electrical contact.

quiz.q: What is the recommended cup size for general TIG welding?
quiz.explanation: A #6 ceramic cup provides good gas coverage for most applications.

quiz.q: What is a common cause of arc wandering?
quiz.explanation: A bent or improperly ground tungsten causes the arc to wander; keep it straight.

quiz.q: Why should you use a heat sink when welding thin metal?
quiz.explanation: A heat sink absorbs excess heat, reducing distortion and burn-through.

quiz.q: What is the correct travel speed for TIG welding?
options: D) Depends on amperage and thickness
quiz.explanation: Travel speed must be adjusted based on material thickness, amperage, and desired bead size.

quiz.q: What is a sign of good penetration in a TIG weld?
options: C) A consistent bead with slight reinforcement
quiz.explanation: A good weld has a smooth, consistent bead with proper fusion and slight reinforcement.

quiz.q: What should you do if you run out of shielding gas mid-weld?
options: B) Stop, replace cylinder, and restart
quiz.explanation: Without shielding gas, the weld will be contaminated; stop and replace the cylinder.

quiz.q: Why is ventilation important in TIG welding?
options: A) To remove ozone and fumes
quiz.explanation: TIG welding produces ozone and metal fumes that can be harmful if inhaled.

quiz.q: What is the first step in the practical exercise?
options: B) Make a bead on plate without filler
quiz.explanation: Practicing a bead on plate helps develop puddle control before adding filler.
